feedback: If a learner expects floating sea ice to raise the gauge: point out the gauge held still, and connect this to displacement — floating ice already pushes aside its own weight of water.
If a learner names only polar ice caps: revisit the component map so glaciers, permafrost, snow cover and sea ice are seen as one worldwide system.
Reinforce the proportion bars: the tiny frozen sliver holds most of Earth's fresh water — not rivers and lakes.
activities.intendedInsight: The cryosphere is a giant connected reservoir holding most of Earth's fresh water; it exchanges water with oceans and atmosphere through the water cycle, and only land-based ice raises sea level when it melts.
learnerActions: Study a display of the planet's water as two proportion bars — a large salty-sea bar and, within the small fresh-water sliver, a bar showing that most fresh water is frozen.
Explore a map of cryosphere components: ice sheets, glaciers, sea ice, permafrost, and snow cover.

Melt components one at a time and observe a sea-level gauge: melting floating Arctic sea ice leaves the gauge still; melting the Greenland and Antarctic ice SHEETS makes it climb toward a marked ~65 m level (per cited sources: Greenland ~7.4 m + Antarctica ~58 m).
Watch water-cycle arrows respond as you act — evaporation, snowfall rebuilding glaciers, and meltwater rivers flowing to the sea — showing ice as a live store, not a static block.
State in your own words why the frozen sliver matters and why only land ice lifts the sea.
activities.title: Frozen Earth console: melt it and watch the system respond

feedback: If a learner predicts the floating cube overflows: run the demo; if the level stays about the same (allowing for small spills or condensation), this shows the floating ice was already displacing its own weight of water.
If a learner thinks melt creates NEW water: connect to states of matter — the same water changes state and location; mass is conserved.
Prompt further thinking: scientists still care about shrinking Arctic sea ice for reasons beyond sea level (e.g. reflecting sunlight, habitat) — invite the learner to reason about why.
Note the limit of the analogy: the spoon/saucer cube isolates displacement only; real land ice melt is driven by many factors, so the demo shows the sea-level rule, not the full cause of melting.
activities.intendedInsight: Floating ice already displaces its own weight of water, so in this fresh-water demo melting it keeps the level about the same (in the salty ocean, melting sea ice adds only a very tiny rise); land-based ice adds new water to the sea. Mass is conserved — melting changes state and location, not the amount of water.
learnerActions: Fill a glass to the brim with water and float an ice cube in it.

Predict, WITH A REASON, whether the glass will overflow as the floating cube melts, then let it melt and observe whether the level changes (it should stay at about the same level; wipe the outside of the glass so condensation is not mistaken for overflow).
Let meltwater from a cube resting on a spoon or saucer lip (standing for land ice) run into the glass, and observe that this overflows.
Compare the two cases and explain why floating ice behaves differently from land ice.
Transfer to a new case: decide whether Greenland's land ice or floating Arctic sea ice matters more for rising seas, and say why.
activities.title: Displacement demo: floating ice vs land ice

feedback: Draw out the land-vs-sea-ice distinction in discussion and ask the learner to explain displacement in their own words.
Follow factual claims with a 'why' so the learner reasons rather than recalls.
activities.intendedInsight: The cryosphere is a connected store at the heart of the water cycle; changes there ripple globally to sea level, currents and water supply.
learnerActions: Listen to or read a short account of the cryosphere's components and its role connecting ice to oceans and atmosphere.
Ask questions and respond: where is most frozen water, and why does only land ice raise the sea?
activities.title: Glaciologist's account of the cryosphere (optional discussion)
